title: Slot in a Sorted Array
statement:
You get an array nums of distinct integers sorted in increasing order, and a number target.

If target is in the array, return its index. If not, return the index where it would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted. Your solution should take O(log n) time.

examples.why: 6 belongs between 5 and 8, so it would take index 2 and push 8 and 11 right.
Bigger than everything: the slot is one past the last index, which is a valid answer.

hints: A linear scan for the first value ≥ target is correct but O(n). The array is sorted, so you can halve the range each step.
You are looking for the first index whose value is ≥ target. If no such index exists, the answer is the length.
Keep a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = length. If nums[mid] < target the answer is right of mid, else it is mid or to its left. Stop when lo = hi.

explain.intuition:
Both cases, found and not found, ask the same question: what is the first index whose value is at least target? If the target is present, that index holds it. If not, that is exactly where it would go. If every value is smaller, the answer is n.

Seen that way, the array splits into a "too small" part and a "big enough" part, and binary search finds the border. Using a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = n lets the answer n fall out naturally, without a special case.
steps: If nums[mid] < target, the border is right of mid: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise hi = mid.
pitfalls: Using hi = n − 1 and returning -1 or mid when the target is missing. That misses the slot after the last element.
Writing hi = mid − 1 with the half-open range. Mid might be the answer itself.
Mixing the closed-range loop (lo ≤ hi) with the half-open updates, which loops forever when lo = hi.

solutions.title: Linear scan
solutions.idea: Walk until the first value that is at least the target.

solutions.title: Lower-bound binary search
solutions.idea: Binary search for the first index whose value is ≥ target, on a half-open range.

followups: Values may repeat. Return the first and the last index of the target. Which comparison changes for the second search?
Python has bisect_left. What does bisect_right return for the same input, and when would you want it?
